title: Loyalists and Native Nations
objective: After this level you can explain why many colonists stayed loyal to Britain and why most Native nations sided with the Crown.
summary: Loyalists, perhaps 15 percent to a third of colonists, sided with the Crown; most Native nations that fought did too, hoping to keep their lands.

cards.headline: Not every American wanted independence.
cards.body: Neighbors split, families split, and an old league of Native nations split too. Who stood by the king, and why?

cards.headline: Who stayed loyal
cards.body: Loyalists came from every colony: royal officeholders, Anglican clergy and their congregations, large landholders, wealthy merchants, and pacifist Quakers. What most shared was a cautious, conservative streak and a deep devotion to Britain and the Crown. Estimates of their numbers range from about 15 percent of colonists to about a third.

cards.headline: The price of losing
cards.body: When the war ended, many Loyalists left for good. Estimates range from about 60,000 to 100,000 people. Most went to Canada, to Nova Scotia, New Brunswick or Quebec.

cards.headline: Why Native nations chose Britain
cards.body: Most Native nations that fought sided with Britain, from old alliances and a belief that they had a better chance of keeping their lands under the British. The Mohawk leader Joseph Brant (Thayendanegea) led Haudenosaunee fighters allied with the British in raids on New York and Pennsylvania settlements.

cards.headline: A league divided
cards.body: The Haudenosaunee Confederacy first tried to stay neutral, then split. The Oneida and Tuscarora backed the Americans; most other nations backed Britain. Oneida allies carried corn to Washington’s starving army at Valley Forge, and an Oneida woman, Polly Cooper, stayed to show soldiers how to cook it.

cards.headline: Left out of the peace
cards.body: In the Treaty of Paris of 1783, neither Britain nor the United States made any provision for their Six Nations allies. Friends and enemies of the Americans alike were left to negotiate on their own.

cards.headline: Loyalists and Native nations: explained
learned: Loyalists: estimates from 15 percent to a third
Most Native nations that fought backed Britain
The peace of 1783 left the Six Nations out

questions.prompt: Where did most Loyalists who left the United States after the war go?

options.label: The Caribbean
options.rationale: Some went there, but most went to Canada.

questions.explanation: Most went to Canada: Nova Scotia, New Brunswick or Quebec.

questions.prompt: How did most Native nations that fought hope siding with Britain would help them?

options.label: It would win their leaders seats in Parliament
It would end the fur trade with the colonies
It gave them a better chance of keeping their lands
It would turn their lands into British colonies
options.rationale: They sought to keep their own lands.

questions.explanation: They believed they had a better chance of keeping their lands under the British.

questions.prompt: Level 6’s Great Law required the Haudenosaunee to decide unanimously. What happened when the Revolution came?

options.label: The nations agreed to join Britain together
The Confederacy dissolved the Great Law in 1776
options.rationale: The split came from disagreement, not a vote.

options.label: The nations could not agree, and the Confederacy split
The nations voted to join the United States
options.rationale: Only two nations backed the Americans.

questions.explanation: Unable to agree, the Confederacy split, with the Oneida and Tuscarora on the American side.
